paras: The attempted lynching of Henry Briggs took place in Chicago on the morning of December 17, 1888, when a crowd of factory workers and passers-by chased a man accused of attempting to assault a young factory employee, crying "Hang him!" Police intervention saved him, and he was later charged before a justice and let off with a fine.
The man gave his name as Henry Briggs; one dispatch called him "an old reprobate," while another said he described himself as a watchman at Battery D. Neither account stated his race.

According to the girl's story, Briggs followed her into the hall of the factory building of Rosenblatt's box factory at 52 Wabash avenue and caught her. The Rock Island Argus gave her age as 15, while the Jasper Courier printed a name that survives only as "Miss Maria Mon-" in its garbled type. Her screams brought help, and Briggs fled.

All the male hands in the factory and many passers-by took up the chase, and in the Argus's words "the chances were good for a lamp-post lynching." The two dispatches describe his rescue differently: the Argus said he ran into a police station and was locked up, while the Jasper item said police on Wabash avenue had to use their clubs to keep the crowd off him.

Briggs was charged before Justice "Whitne" with attempting a criminal assault. Because there was "some question as to his identity," he was let off with a fine, printed as $30. No report of action against members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

The episode reached the white press as brief Chicago wire items printed outside the city. The Rock Island Argus ran it on December 18 under the headline "A Miscreant Saved by Police," treating the accusation as fact with phrases such as "a bold attempt at outrage" and casting the police as having saved a guilty man. The Jasper Weekly Courier of Indiana printed a different version on December 28 under "A Narrow Escape," giving the charge as the girl's story and adding the fine and the doubt about his identity.

Whether Briggs reached safety by running into a police station, as the Argus reported, or was shielded on the street by police swinging clubs, as the Jasper item reported, is not settled by the two dispatches.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Briggs
bases: Both dispatches describe a crowd pursuing a man accused of assaulting a factory girl with cries to hang him, stopped only by police (A1, A2).
A crowd of factory hands and passers-by chased Briggs crying 'Hang him!' over an alleged assault, but police intervened and he was not killed (A1, A2); it was an attempted lynching.

Two differently worded Chicago dispatches (dated Dec. 17 and Dec. 18) agree that a crowd tried to lynch Henry Briggs after an alleged assault on a Rosenblatt factory employee and that police saved him, though they differ on details (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Chicago dispatch, Dec. 18 (Rock Island Argus)
accounts.gist: Briggs attempted 'outrage' on a girl of 15 in the factory hall; chased by factory hands and passers-by crying 'Hang him!', he ran into a police station and was locked up.

accounts.label: Chicago dispatch, Dec. 17 (Jasper Courier)
accounts.gist: Briggs narrowly escaped lynching on Wabash avenue as police clubbed back the crowd; charged before a justice, he was fined because his identity was in question.

framing.detail: The Argus treated the accusation as fact ('a bold attempt at outrage', 'old reprobate', 'miscreant') while presenting the near-lynching as a rescue: 'A Miscreant Saved by Police'.
The Jasper Courier ran a brief wire item headed 'A Narrow Escape', stating the charge and the girl's story without comment.
